newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat, Mubarak coordinate views ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, Mubarak coordinate views ahead of summit.

text.p: A summit between leaders of Egypt and Israel planned for Tuesday faces grave differences over Jewish settlements in occupied Arab lands but it aims to pave the way for the Middle East peace process to resume.
Officials do not expect a breakthrough from the meeting between Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh.
Mubarak and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat held two hours of talks to coordinate their views ahead of the summit.

"The Palestinians say they cannot negotiate against a background of fait accomplis and the continuation of settlements. Our job is to deal with that in order to pave the way for the resumption of a positive atmosphere which will enable us to save the peace process," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told reporters after the meeting.

"We're going to talk to him (Netanyahu) and we're going to listen to what he has to say or wishes to say and we hope that things will move. Arafat has articulated his point of view to us very well in tonight's meeting," Moussa said.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk said he did not expect a breakthrough.

"We do not expect a dramatic breakthrough...but a better understanding towards the way in which Israel, Egypt, the Palestinians and the United States will continue to advance the peace process," Israel's domestic news agency Itim quoted Indyk as saying.
"We do not want failure but I caution against expectations which are too high."

Palestinian-Israeli peacemaking was halted in March when Israel started building the Jewish settlement of Har Homa in Arab East Jerusalem. Israel captured the area in 1967 but its subsequent annexation was not recognised by most countries.

Palestinians see the work at the site they call Jabal Abu Ghneim as pre-empting final status talks on the east of the city, which they see as the capital of a future state. Israel says the entire city is its capital.
Mediator Egypt supports the Palestinian view that they will only resume talks when Israel halts work on the settlement.
But Netanyahu told Israel Army Radio after being asked about reports of a possible settlement freeze: "It is not on the agenda -- not on mine."

"The meeting will be a crossroads. Either the beginning of a denouement or leaving matters to get worse," an Arab analyst said of what would be the fourth meeting between Mubarak and Netanyahu since the rightwing Israeli took office in June 1996.
Moussa had said the summit would succeed if Israel agreed to stop building settlements. Mubarak said last week a six-month suspension of settlement building could revive the process.

Israel predicted the summit could make limited progress on ending the crisis. "Israel has not offered to stop work on the Har Homa neighbourhood. We are not proposing it," Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said.
